To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the occurrence and magnitude (peak discharge) of floods are controlled by catchment storage thresholds, (b) the flood frequency curve can exhibit multiple breaks in slope, and (c) the inclusion of infrequently occurring summer storm events increases both the temporal frequency and magnitude of flood occurrence, thus contributing to a steeper flood frequency curve, and an additional slope break.

Thresholds in runoff generation mechanisms (e.g. from subsurface to surface runoff) are shown to have an impact on the shape of the flood frequency curves, as well as their temporal occurrence and magnitude.

(1) thresholds in catchment storage can be identified as a break in the flood frequency curves; (2) tropical cyclones can increase the temporal frequency of flood events; (3) tropical cyclones are also associated with a break in the slope in the flood frequency distribution; (4) tropical cyclones have an effect on the magnitude of the floods; and (5) tropical cyclones may be a factor contributing to the increase in flood frequency and magnitude.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of catchment thresholds on flood frequency and the implications of these effects for flood frequency estimation.
how rainfall variability and catchment threshold nonlinearities interact, to influence the occurrence and magnitude distributions of flood events.
the impact of thresholds upon flood frequency, and the implications this has for the occurrence and magnitude (i.e. peak discharge) of flood events.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the flood frequency curves are strongly influenced by the catchment threshold effects.
thresholds are an important feature in the rainfall-run-off process and that they have a significant impact upon flood frequency curves.

the inclusion of thresholds, in particular those associated with runoff generation, and the inclusion of infrequently occurring extreme events (i.e. tropical cyclones) are important factors in the generation of flood frequency curves.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the flood frequency curve is a function of rainfall variability, and the threshold behaviour associated with the catchment storage.

the flood frequency curve is a complex product of the rainfall-runoff system and its thresholds, as well as the rainfall variability, and that the flood frequency is not a simple linear function of rainfall intensity.
the occurrence and magnitude distribution of floods are strongly dependent on the threshold storage in the catchment, the rainfall variability and the rainfall-runoff processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the flood frequency curve is sensitive to the rainfall-runoff processes, in particular, to the occurrence of threshold nonlinearities in runoff generation.

the flood frequency curve can be used to identify threshold effects in catchment behaviour, and that this information can be used as an aid to the interpretation and understanding of catchment response.
flood frequency curves can have multiple breaks in slope, and these breaks are not always related to the occurrence and magnitude frequency distributions.
